commentary: The market looks calm on the surface and is churning violently underneath. The S&P 500 sits comfortably above its long-term trend line, but the stocks that led this rally - chips, AI servers, data-center hardware - are down 12 to 20 percent in a month while the index barely moved. Tonight's headlines tell the story: SoftBank down 9 percent, Micron plunging, chip stocks selling off across Asia. That is money quietly leaving the trade everyone crowded into, and it is the same trade that cost me money on Dell and HPE last week, so I am not going back for a third helping. The top of my scan is cybersecurity - four stocks up more than 100 percent in three months, every one of them now trading above what Wall Street analysts think they are worth. That is not an opportunity; that is a queue. Instead I am buying Abbott, the medical-device maker, with about 14 percent of the account. Abbott fell 28 percent since February because investors feared that expiring health-insurance subsidies would make people skip medical procedures. Yesterday Abbott reported and the fear did not show up in the numbers: device sales grew 8.4 percent, glucose monitors grew 11 percent, and management raised its profit forecast for the year. The insight is that Abbott's biggest device business sells continuous glucose monitors to people who already have diabetes - a recurring purchase, not an elective surgery someone postpones - so the subsidy math consensus applied to it never fit. The stock jumped 10 percent on heavy volume and is still 26 percent below its high. What would change my mind: rival device makers report starting July 29, and if they show the procedure slowdown that Abbott did not, I am wrong and I exit. I will also sell if Abbott falls back to $93 and gives up the breakout. I am honest about the weak spot here - the buying pressure under this stock was negative right up until yesterday, so this is one good day, not yet a trend, which is exactly why the stop is close and the position is one percent of my money at risk.

**Improvement note:** Two concrete data defects cost me real research time and nearly cost me a bad trade.

1. **The `post_earnings_drift_candidate` gap test has a hole that fires false positives on distribution bars.** It flagged UNH `gap_held_revisions_up` because the close held above the *pre-gap close* — but UNH printed a 52-week high at ~$460 and closed at $423.38, giving back nearly the entire 10% advance on 2x volume. That is the *opposite* of the institutional-urgency signal the flag is meant to capture. The fix is one line: require the close to sit in the **upper half of the day's range** (`(close - low) / (high - low) > 0.5`) before `gap_held` can be true. Without it, the flag rewards exactly the failed prints the playbook says to avoid, and only reading the chart image caught it. UNH scored 6.06 and was the sole PED candidate on the board — a less careful run buys it.

2. **`momentum_health` is missing from this bundle entirely**, so the validator's automatic new-BUY size-halving could not fire during what is plainly a momentum unwind (MTUM -12.1% off its peak, SPMO -10.1%, vs SPY -0.9%). The raw data was sitting right there in `data/cache/momentum_etfs.json` — the block just never made it into `brain_slim_v1`. This is a fail-open on a safety feature, which is the worst kind: it is silent. Worth checking whether `runlib/context_tiers.py` (modified in the working tree) drops the key, and adding an assertion that a missing `momentum_health` logs loudly rather than passing as `unknown`.

Weekly self-review: This week was mostly build week, not trade week - the system went from a bare skeleton to a full pipeline (data relay, validator, position sizing, watchlist triggers, insider activity, sector relative strength, post-earnings drift detection) in a handful of commits, and only opened its first two live paper positions on 7/9 (DELL) and 7/10 (HPE). Neither has closed yet, so there is no win/loss to grade - the real test of the process comes next week when these mature past a few days and I have to apply the cash-test and thesis-break discipline for real, not just in theory. What I got right: discipline held under pressure - six separate runs today all correctly said no-trade rather than forcing a mediocre setup into a rate-driven, breadth-thin tape, and both live entries were valuation-anchored (12-20x forward earnings) rather than chases into the 40-170x names topping the momentum scan. What went wrong was mostly data quality, not reasoning: the insider Form-4 feed got flagged as noisy five separate times this week because financial-sponsor distributions (Silver Lake's Dell unwind, ALAB's post-lockup sales) bury genuine officer-conviction signals under hundreds of routine rows, a stale next_earnings field showed a past date for HPE, and the post_earnings_drift_candidate flag missed HPE's textbook drift setup because a one-time GAAP charge masked rising estimates - all bad data, not bad judgment, but they cost research time I'd rather spend on names. ** The insider_activity feed is dominated by financial-sponsor unwinds (Silver Lake's programmatic Dell distribution ran to 79 separate line items) and routine 10b5-1 officer sales, which bury any genuinely informative *open-market* signal. A pre-computed classifier flag distinguishing "sponsor/PE distribution" and "scheduled 10b5-1" from "discretionary open-market officer buy/sell," plus a net cluster-buy score, would let me weight this data in seconds instead of scrolling hundreds of near-identical sell tickets to conclude "no signal."

** The insider_activity feed lumps financial-sponsor distributions (Silver Lake's DELL unwind, ALAB's pre-arranged director sales) in with genuine operating-insider signals, forcing me to manually parse dozens of near-identical rows to conclude "not a real signal." A pre-computed classification — tagging each cluster as sponsor/10b5-1-scheduled vs. discretionary officer transaction, and netting to a single per-ticker signal — would make the "clustered officer buying vs. routine selling" judgment the rules ask for far faster and less error-prone.

** The `post_earnings_drift_candidate` flag was `false` for HPE even though it fits the textbook drift profile the bundle prioritizes (record quarter just reported, +40% EPS revisions, price still 24% below its high). The detector appears to have been distorted by HPE's GAAP net *loss* last quarter — a one-time Juniper acquisition charge — which masked the underlying estimate momentum. Adding a "GAAP charge / acquisition-adjusted" screen (or keying the drift flag off EPS-revision magnitude and days-since-earnings rather than reported net income sign) would have surfaced this run's best idea automatically instead of leaving me to reconstruct it by hand.

** The context bundle's per-candidate `next_earnings` field is unreliable — HPE's showed `2026-06-01` (already past) while the `days_to_earnings`/`days_since_earnings` fields correctly implied the next print is in September. These two sources disagreeing forced me to reason around it; the run would be cleaner if `next_earnings` were validated to always be a *future* date (or dropped in favor of the days-based fields), so the earnings-clock gate can't be tripped by a stale value.

** The `insider_activity` feed is dominated by non-signal noise — Silver Lake's sponsor-distribution selling in DELL and Alba/Dyckerhoff post-lockup selling in ALAB swamp the data with hundreds of routine rows, which buries any genuinely informative *officer* buying/selling. This run would have been sharper if the context bundle pre-classified Form 4s (e.g., tagging financial-sponsor/10%-owner distributions and post-IPO-lockup sales separately from discretionary open-market C-suite transactions) and surfaced a net "discretionary officer" buy/sell tally per ticker, so clustered insider *conviction* signals aren't drowned out by mechanical unwinds.

** The context bundle gives me valuation and price/momentum but no consensus estimates or forward revenue-growth figures, so I'm forced to lean on trailing fundamentals plus headline sentiment when judging whether a rich multiple (ANET at 41x, ALAB at 97x) is justified. Adding forward revenue-growth and EPS-revision (analyst estimate trend) fields per candidate would materially sharpen the "is this multiple deserved" call and reduce reliance on qualitative news vibes — the single biggest lever on proposal quality this run.

** The context bundle deep-researches only the top-5 by deterministic score, but two of those five (TXN, AMD) are effectively un-actionable this run because of earnings timing (7/22) or a same-day news gap — meaning I burned my richest data (filings, 13F, news) on names I won't trade, while candidates like HPE and CRDO that I'm actively weighing had only a price and momentum row. Adding a `next_earnings` field and a `days_to_earnings` flag directly into the `universe_scan.top_setups` rows (not just the news block), plus expanding SEC/news enrichment to the top 8 rather than top 5, would let me screen out earnings-binary setups before spending research budget and give me fundamentals on the names I actually end up considering.

** This run would have been materially better with two data additions to the context bundle: (1) a **forward valuation field per candidate** (P/E or EV/S vs. its own 1-yr history) — right now I'm inferring "extended" purely from price momentum, when the real question for the CPI/rate-driven multiple-compression thesis is whether valuations are stretched, and (2) **intraday/1-day price change** so I can distinguish a name resting after a run from one spiking on news *today* (AMD) without cross-referencing headline timestamps by hand. Adding a `pct_change_1d` to the price block and a `valuation` sub-object to each `top_setups` entry would sharpen entry-timing judgment on exactly the chase-vs-wait decisions that dominated this cycle.
